az_north_suess.blurb: North Suess is a small bouldering zone in Crozier Canyon, in northern Arizona, at roughly 4,800 feet. It is the larger of the two sections of the Seuss Area and holds most of its problems, with less brush to fight through than the southern section. It has five problems, all in the V4 to V5 range, so it suits climbers already comfortable on moderate-to-hard boulders rather than beginners. Reaching it takes about ten minutes on foot from where you leave the car beside the dirt road.

az_paleface_slab.blurb: Paleface Slab is a clean, low-key face in the West Stronghold of Cochise Stronghold, in the Dragoon Mountains of southern Arizona, at around 5,700 feet. It has five routes: four bolted lines and one trad line, spanning easy fifth class through the 5.10 range. That makes it a reasonable pick for a mixed party, with a couple of gentle leads and a few harder sport pitches. Descent is by rappel off shared anchors, so bring two long ropes. The walk in leaves a wash and follows a faint path up a ridge, and it is easy to wander into the boulder fields if you are not watching for the route.
az_paleface_slab.parking_note: Drive the Forest Road 687 dirt track all the way to its end, where the lot serves several nearby domes and the slab. The road is rough, but a passenger car can manage it if driven slowly.

az_pontatoc_ridge.blurb: Pontatoc Ridge is a secluded, northwest-facing cliff above Pontatoc Canyon on the Santa Catalina side of Mount Lemmon, within sight of the Tucson trailhead lot at about 4,300 feet. It carries five long, committing lines, mostly traditional with a single bolted one, running from the 5.8 range up to 5.11. These are multi-pitch objectives of six to ten pitches, not quick crag laps. The route to the base is a steep, loose bushwhack up a drainage, so expect a slow, effortful walk before you even rope up. It suits experienced parties after a quiet backcountry day.
az_pontatoc_ridge.parking_note: Park in the Finger Rock trailhead lot at the north end of Alvernon Way in Tucson; the cliff can be seen from the lot.

az_roadside_boulder.blurb: Roadside Boulder sits beside the road near the Marshall Gulch picnic area on Mount Lemmon, close to Summerhaven and the Aspen Trail Boulders. It is a single block with five problems spread from the very easiest grade up to V8, so there is a warm-up for newcomers and a couple of hard lines for strong climbers. A small stream runs through the landing for much of the year, which is worth knowing before you lay out pads. It is described as usually in shape in the summer before the monsoon and again in late fall. A short stroll from the car gets you there.

az_rock_of_no_name.blurb: Rock of No Name is a small south-facing crag in the Bear Canyon area of Mount Lemmon, in the Santa Catalinas near Tucson, at about 6,400 feet. It lies just beyond Paradox Rock, and the approach is shared with that crag. Climbing here is traditional only, with five lines from moderate fifth class to 5.9, so it suits a party that wants easy-to-middling leads without any bolts to clip. Placing your own gear is the norm, aside from a single anchor high on the face. The wider canyon is shaded by tall pines.

az_skillsaw_crag.blurb: Skillsaw Crag is a compact cliff at about 7,000 feet on Mount Lemmon, within the Windy Ridge zone of the Santa Catalinas near Tucson. It holds five climbs, a blend of three bolted and two trad lines, with grades from 5.10 up to 5.12, so it is a place for confident leaders rather than novices. The walk is almost nothing: cross the road from the pullout used for neighboring crags and head to the Matterhorn Boulder, with the cliff a few steps beyond. At this altitude, spring and fall tend to be the comfortable seasons for the wider area.
